result: K13 genotyping of 3,257 African samples from 11 countries (2011-2019) revealed that 98% were wild-type, with only 35 unique non-synonymous mutations identified. Only two mutations were present in ≥10 samples: R561H (n=20, exclusively in Rwanda, 2% of all Rwandan samples) and A578S (n=10).
evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C31, and C33 provide consistent genotyping data from a large sample set across multiple African countries. The data clearly document the low prevalence of K13 mutations in Africa, with specific quantification of mutation frequencies. The methodology is appropriate for surveillance studies.

result: Gene editing of K13 mutations (R561H, M579I, C580Y) into African parasite strains revealed strain-dependent resistance phenotypes. In 3D7, R561H conferred highest RSA survival (6.6%), while M579I and C580Y showed 4.8% survival. F32 showed no significant resistance with any mutation (0.3-0.5% survival). UG815 showed highest resistance levels (~12% for both M579I and C580Y), while UG659 showed moderate resistance.
evaluation: Claims C36-C44 present comprehensive RSA data across multiple African strains with appropriate controls (C38). The data demonstrate clear strain-dependent effects with statistical significance indicated. Western blot data (C39) provides mechanistic support showing ~30% reduction in K13 protein levels. Multiple independent clones and replicates strengthen the findings.

result: Fitness assays using qPCR-based allelic discrimination revealed that K13 mutations conferred variable fitness costs in African strains. M579I and C580Y showed significant fitness defects in most strains (largest in 3D7 and UG815, minimal in UG659). R561H showed no fitness cost in 3D7 but significant cost in F32. Fitness costs ranged from <1% to 12% per generation, with high RSA survival generally correlating with high fitness costs, except for 3D7R561H and UG659C580Y.
evaluation: Claims C45-C51 present fitness data from co-culture competition assays over 36 days (18 generations) using validated qPCR methodology. The data show clear trends with appropriate quantification of fitness costs. The correlation analysis (C51) identifies important exceptions that have epidemiological implications. Multiple replicates and time points strengthen the conclusions.

result: K13 genotyping of 3,327 Cambodian samples (2001-2017) revealed 19 non-synonymous mutations, with only three present in >10 samples (Y493H, R539T, C580Y). The C580Y mutation swept across all four regions of Cambodia, reaching nearly 100% prevalence in western and southern regions by 2016-2017. In 2001-2002, western Cambodia already showed 44% mutant prevalence (56% wild-type), while northern/eastern regions were 96% wild-type.
evaluation: Claims C52-C60 present comprehensive spatio-temporal surveillance data from Cambodia with large sample sizes across multiple years and regions. The data clearly document the emergence and spread of C580Y, with striking temporal trends. The observation that C580Y was already prevalent before clinical reports of delayed clearance (C56-C57) is particularly notable.

result: Gene editing of K13 mutations into Asian strains (Dd2 and Cam3.II) revealed mutation-specific and strain-dependent resistance. In Dd2, P553L and R561H showed RSA survival comparable to C580Y (~4.3-4.7%), while F446I and P574L showed modest increases (2.0-2.1%). E252Q showed no resistance. R539T showed highest resistance (20.0%). In Cam3.II, R561H showed higher resistance than C580Y (13.2% vs 10.0%), while F446I, P553L, and P574L showed no significant increases.
evaluation: Claims C64-C70 present systematic RSA data across multiple mutations in two Asian strains with appropriate controls. The data demonstrate clear mutation-specific and strain-dependent effects with statistical significance. The finding that R561H exceeds C580Y in Cam3.II is particularly important. Multiple replicates support the conclusions.

result: eGFP-based fitness assays in Dd2 parasites revealed that F446I, P553L, and C580Y mutations resulted in minimal fitness costs, while E252Q, R561H, and P574L showed greater costs. C580Y and P553L provided optimal combinations of elevated RSA survival and minimal fitness costs. All fitness costs in Dd2 were considerably lower than in most African lines.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 present fitness data using a validated eGFP-based competition assay over 20 days (10 generations). The methodology differs from the African strain assays but is appropriate for the Dd2 background. The comparison to African strains (C74) is supported by data from both assay systems. The identification of optimal resistance/fitness combinations has important epidemiological implications.

result: Gene editing of K13 mutations into five Thai isolates revealed major genetic background effects, with C580Y yielding RSA survival rates ranging from 2.1% to 15.4%. R561H consistently showed moderate to high resistance at or above C580Y levels. E252Q editing showed no significant resistance, but two unedited Thai isolates naturally expressing E252Q showed RSA survival above 1% threshold (2.7% and 5.1%), suggesting additional genetic factors are required for E252Q-mediated resistance.
evaluation: Claims C75-C79 present systematic data across multiple Thai strains demonstrating genetic background effects. The comparison between edited and unedited E252Q lines (C77-C79) provides strong evidence for multigenic resistance. The inference in C79 is well-supported by the contrasting phenotypes. Multiple replicates strengthen the conclusions.

result: CRISPR/Cas9 editing to revert fd D193Y and mdr2 T484I mutations in K13 C580Y Cambodian strains (RF7 and Cam3.II) showed no impact on RSA survival rates or parasite fitness. Isogenic lines with mutant or wild-type fd/mdr2 alleles showed equivalent RSA survival (~27% for RF7, ~19-22% for Cam3.II) and no fitness differences in eGFP competition assays.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 present definitive gene editing experiments directly testing the role of fd and mdr2 mutations. The use of isogenic lines with appropriate controls (silent shield mutations) provides strong evidence. RSA data across multiple DHA concentrations (C81) and fitness assays at different starting ratios strengthen the negative findings. The conclusion (C85) that these are markers rather than functional determinants is well-supported.

result: The K13 R561H mutation, initially identified at 2% prevalence in Rwanda (2012-2015), increased to 12-13% prevalence by 2018-2019 and was associated with delayed parasite clearance in patients treated with artemether-lumefantrine.
evaluation: Claims C23, C91, and C92 document the temporal increase in R561H prevalence in Rwanda with appropriate citations. The association with delayed clearance (C92) is supported by clinical data from cited studies. This represents important surveillance data documenting emergence of resistance in Africa.

result: K13 mutations can confer ART resistance across multiple Asian and African strains at levels varying widely by mutation and genetic background. African strains showed stronger fitness costs compared to Asian parasites, potentially predicting slower dissemination in high-transmission settings. However, R561H confers elevated RSA survival with minimal fitness cost in African 3D7 parasites.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 represent the main conclusions synthesizing data from multiple experiments (RSA and fitness assays across strains). These summary claims are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented in the manuscript. The prediction about slower dissemination (C25) is appropriately qualified as speculation based on fitness data.

result: Certain African strains present no major biological obstacle to becoming ART resistant in vitro upon acquiring K13 mutations. However, K13 C580Y may not easily establish in Africa due to polyclonal infections generating intra-host competition, and high acquired immunity in endemic settings potentially minimizing infection by unfit parasites.
evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by RSA data showing resistance in some African strains. However, claims C87-C88 are largely speculative, extrapolating from in vitro fitness data to predict population-level dynamics. While the reasoning is plausible and cites relevant epidemiological knowledge, these predictions lack direct empirical support from field studies or transmission experiments.

result: C580Y was at high prevalence in western Cambodia before first clinical reports of delayed clearance. The success of C580Y cannot be explained by resistance alone, as R539T and I543T confer greater resistance. C580Y shows minimal fitness cost in Dd2, similar to P553L, yet P553L has been far less successful regionally. Additional factors beyond resistance and fitness, such as specific genetic backgrounds or partner drug selection, likely contributed to C580Y's dominance.
evaluation: Claims C93-C100 integrate surveillance data (C93) with experimental resistance (C94) and fitness data (C97-C98) to address the puzzle of C580Y's success. The comparison with P553L (C98-C99) strengthens the argument that resistance and fitness alone are insufficient explanations. The speculation about additional factors (C100) is appropriately qualified and supported by citations.

result: No evident association was observed between genotypes of pfcrt, mdr1, arps10, ap-2μ, or ubp1 and the degree to which mutant K13 conferred ART resistance in vitro across African and Asian strains tested.
evaluation: Claim C105 reports negative findings from genotype-phenotype correlation analysis across the strain panel. While the manuscript references Supplementary file 4 for the data, the systematic genotyping and phenotyping of multiple strains provides appropriate evidence for this negative result. However, the analysis is correlative and cannot definitively rule out roles for these genes.

result: In Dd2 parasites, E252Q and R561H showed the most detrimental fitness impacts and were later overtaken by C580Y in the Thailand-Myanmar border region. C580Y produced an optimal combination of no measurable fitness cost and relatively high RSA survival in Dd2. However, in a prior independent study using Thai NHP4302 strain, R561H showed slightly improved fitness relative to C580Y.
evaluation: Claims C101-C103 integrate fitness data from this study with historical surveillance data and prior published work. The data support the fitness differences in Dd2 (C101-C102). The citation of contrasting results in a different strain (C103) appropriately acknowledges strain-dependent effects and strengthens the overall conclusion about genetic background importance.

result: Malaria remains a major global health problem with 229 million cases and 409,000 deaths in 2019, primarily in Sub-Saharan Africa from P. falciparum. The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has compromised malaria control. In the absence of an effective vaccine, control relies on ACTs, which pair fast-acting artemisinin derivatives with longer-lasting partner drugs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide background context with appropriate citations to WHO reports and established literature. These claims accurately represent the current state of malaria epidemiology and treatment, providing necessary context for the study.

result: ART resistance has swept across Southeast Asia, first emerging in western Cambodia. Clinically, it manifests as delayed parasite clearance (half-life >5.5 hr vs <2-3 hr for sensitive parasites) without treatment failure if partner drugs remain effective. In vitro, resistance is measured by the RSA. ART-resistant strains have also acquired PPQ resistance, with failure rates exceeding 50% in parts of Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam.
evaluation: Claims C7-C13 provide essential background on ART resistance with appropriate citations to key studies. These claims accurately describe the clinical and laboratory manifestations of resistance and the current situation in Southeast Asia, establishing the rationale for the study.

result: ART resistance is primarily determined by mutations in the K13 beta-propeller domain, which reduce hemoglobin endocytosis and Fe2+-heme release, decreasing ART activation. C580Y is the most prevalent mutation in SE Asia and mediates resistance in vitro. Nearly 200 other K13 mutations have been documented, but only a handful (N458Y, M476I, Y493H, R539T, I543T, R561H) have been validated by gene editing. Mutations in fd and mdr2 have been associated with resistance.
evaluation: Claims C14-C21 provide comprehensive background on K13-mediated resistance with extensive citations to prior work. These claims accurately summarize the current understanding of resistance mechanisms and the validation status of various mutations, establishing the knowledge gap that this study addresses.

result: Of the 35 non-synonymous K13 mutations identified in African samples, only M476I and R561H have been validated as resistance mediators in the SE Asian Dd2 strain. A578S was previously shown not to confer resistance in Dd2. 3D7 segregates phylogenetically with Rwandan parasites, while F32 was derived from Tanzania.
evaluation: Claims C30, C32, C34, and C35 provide context for strain selection and prior validation status with appropriate citations. These claims establish the rationale for testing specific mutations in specific strains and are well-supported by cited literature and phylogenetic analysis.

result: Previously, introduction of M476I into F32 resulted in modest resistance (1.7% survival), while the same mutation conferred ~10% survival in Dd2.
evaluation: Claim C41 cites prior work (Straimer et al., 2015) to provide context for the current F32 results. This comparison strengthens the argument for genetic background effects and is appropriately cited.

result: Y493H, R539T, and C580Y mutations were previously shown to confer ART resistance in vitro. Delayed parasite clearance was first documented in 2008-2009. F446I is predominant in Myanmar. P553L, R561H, and P574L have multiple independent origins in SE Asia. E252Q was formerly prevalent on the Thai-Myanmar border and has been associated with delayed clearance despite being upstream of the propeller domain.
evaluation: Claims C54, C57, C61-C63 provide background context for mutation selection with appropriate citations. These claims accurately represent prior knowledge about specific mutations and their geographic distributions, establishing rationale for testing these variants.

result: In a prior genome-wide association study of SE Asian parasites, K13-mediated ART resistance was associated with fd D193Y and mdr2 T484I mutations.
evaluation: Claim C80 accurately cites prior GWAS findings (Miotto et al., 2015) that motivated the gene editing experiments to test fd and mdr2 roles. This provides appropriate context for the negative findings reported in this study.

result: Fitness costs from PfCRT mutations led to rapid resurgence of wild-type parasites after chloroquine use in Africa. The M579I mutation was detected in Equatorial Guinea with in vivo ART resistance but was absent in all 3,257 African samples in this study.
evaluation: Claims C89-C90 provide relevant historical context (C89) and connect prior case reports (C90) to current surveillance data. The absence of M579I in the large sample set, combined with its high fitness cost, supports the interpretation about fitness constraints on resistance spread.

result: F446I has spread across Myanmar despite conferring low-level resistance. In a separate gene editing study, F446I yielded no significant resistance in 3D7 and was fitness neutral, consistent with findings in Dd2.
evaluation: Claims C95-C96 integrate current findings with prior work (Siddiqui et al., 2020) and surveillance data (Imwong et al., 2020). The consistency across studies and strains strengthens the conclusion that F446I's spread cannot be explained by high-level resistance, highlighting the complexity of resistance evolution.

result: The manuscript discusses potential secondary genetic determinants (fd, mdr2, ap-2μ, ubp1, pfcoronin) and DNA repair mutations that might augment resistance. P. falciparum genomic structures in Africa are more diverse than Cambodia, potentially slowing resistance spread. Reduced transmission and declining immunity in some African areas may benefit mutant K13 emergence. Lumefantrine remains effective in Africa, contrasting with SE Asia where PPQ resistance enables multidrug-resistant strain dissemination. Recent surveillance shows low K13 mutation prevalence in Africa, but R561H emergence in Rwanda requires monitoring for potential partner drug resistance and treatment failure.
evaluation: Claims C104-C114 largely represent speculation and discussion of future research directions with appropriate citations. While the reasoning is sound and based on established principles, these claims make predictions about future events (C108, C110, C114) or discuss potential mechanisms (C104, C106, C109) that lack direct experimental support in this study. The surveillance data (C113) is supported, but the interpretation about future implications (C114) is speculative.
